did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with a title containing the words “For the director of music. To the tune of ‘The Death of the Son’” and attributes it to David. The title indicates that this is a psalm intended for singing or performance, but the meaning of the phrase “The Death of the Son” is not explained in the body of the psalm.

Did you know? The psalmist emphasizes that he will give thanks to the LORD “with all my heart,” and promises to tell of all His wonderful deeds—meaning that his thanksgiving includes both personal emotion and publicizing the LORD’s works.
Did you know? According to the psalm, the enemies retreat and fall when they come before the LORD: they turn back, stumble, and perish in His presence.
Did you know? The LORD is portrayed as sitting on the throne of judgment and judging fairly. Divine judgment is presented as the basis for the psalmist’s deliverance and vindication.

Did you know? In contrast to the enemies and their cities, whose memory fades away, the LORD “sits enthroned forever.” Thus, the psalm creates a contrast between the transience of the wicked and the permanence of the LORD’s judgment.
Did you know? One of the psalm’s central descriptions is that the LORD is “a stronghold for the oppressed”—a refuge for the weak and suffering, especially in times of trouble.
Did you know? The psalm calls on the people of Zion not to be content with private song, but to proclaim among the nations the LORD’s deeds. Thanksgiving thus becomes a public testimony to His works.

Did you know? The LORD is portrayed as the one who avenges the blood of the afflicted and remembers the cry of the poor and oppressed. In this way, the psalm emphasizes that suffering and injustice are not forgotten before Him.
Did you know? The psalm presents the principle that the wicked are caught by their own actions: the nations sink into the pit and are ensnared in the net they themselves have set.

Did you know? Alongside its description of judgment, the psalm emphasizes that “the needy will not be forgotten forever.” The hope of the poor is presented as a hope that should not perish forever, and the psalmist asks the LORD to rise up and judge the nations.
